market_context: United States; large chicken eggs and variable retail prices
title: Eggs as an affordable source of protein

seo.title: Eggs as an affordable protein source: what you really get
seo.meta_description: One large egg has about 6–7 g protein. See how many eggs provide 20 g, how to calculate cost, and how eggs compare with beans, chicken, and tuna.
seo.search_intent: Evaluate eggs as an affordable protein source using real serving size, local price, protein concentration, and the nutrients in the yolk.

excerpt: One large egg provides about 6–7 g protein and 70–80 calories; three large eggs provide roughly 19 g protein. Eggs are not always the cheapest protein, but they combine moderate cost, convenience, high-quality protein, and micronutrients.
content_html:
Eggs rarely beat chicken breast or tuna for protein per 100 g, but they have a different economic advantage: they come pre-portioned, cook in minutes, keep well under refrigeration, and combine protein with micronutrients at a price that is often moderate.

One large egg provides about 6–7 g protein and 70–80 calories. Two eggs supply roughly 12–14 g protein; three provide about 19 g. Reaching approximately 20 g protein with whole eggs therefore takes around three large eggs.

Price per dozen is less useful than price per protein serving

Egg prices vary by size, production method, store, and week. To compare eggs with another food, calculate what three eggs cost or, more precisely, the price of 20 g protein.

If a dozen costs $3.00, each egg is $0.25. Three eggs cost $0.75 and provide roughly 19 g protein. If the dozen costs $4.20, the same three eggs cost $1.05. The nutrition is nearly unchanged while the economics move substantially.

Whole eggs contribute more than protein

The yolk contains most of the egg’s choline, vitamin B12, vitamin A, selenium, and fat. The white is mostly water and protein.

Replacing every whole egg with whites improves protein per calorie, but it is not a universal nutritional upgrade. A combination—two whole eggs plus extra whites, for example—can raise protein while keeping much of the yolk’s nutrient package.

Compared with legumes, eggs play a different role

Three large eggs provide about 19 g protein and essentially no fiber. A cup of cooked lentils provides roughly 18 g protein and 15.6 g fiber, plus substantially more carbohydrate and food volume.

That makes the phrase “affordable protein” more nuanced than it sounds. Eggs with whole-grain toast and vegetables serve a different meal function from a bowl of lentils.

Compared with chicken or tuna, eggs are less protein concentrated

Cooked chicken breast can provide about 31 g protein per 100 g, while whole egg is closer to 12–13 g. Drained water-packed tuna commonly exceeds 20 g protein per 100 g.

Getting 30 g protein from whole eggs would take roughly 4–5 large eggs, while about 3.5–4 ounces of chicken or tuna can approach that amount. For maximum protein concentration, other foods are more efficient.

Where eggs gain ground: low waste and convenience

An egg can be used one at a time. There is no need to thaw a package or open a large container, so a household can cook exactly one, two, or three. That portion control can reduce food waste.

Eggs also fit inexpensive meals: vegetable omelets, eggs with beans, fried rice with leftover vegetables, or a hard-cooked egg added to a grain bowl. In those dishes, the egg completes the meal rather than having to provide every gram of protein.

Are eggs always the cheapest protein?

No. Dry beans and lentils often cost less per gram of protein; sale-priced chicken, milk, yogurt, peanut butter, or canned fish can also beat eggs depending on the store.

The strength of eggs is the package of reasonable cost, high-quality protein, micronutrients, storage life, and almost no advance preparation. In many kitchens, that combination matters more than winning by a few cents.

faq.question: How many eggs provide 20 grams of protein?
faq.answer: One large egg has about 6–7 g protein, so three eggs provide roughly 19 g and come close to 20 g.

faq.question: Are eggs cheaper than beans for protein?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Dry beans and lentils often have a very low cost per gram of protein and also provide fiber. Local prices determine the comparison.

faq.question: Are egg whites a better value than whole eggs?
faq.answer: It depends on price. Whites provide more protein per calorie, while whole eggs include the yolk, which contains choline, vitamins, minerals, and fat.
